title: Banner Ad Sizes 2026: Standard Display Ad Sizes Chart
summary: Standard banner and display ad sizes in pixels, with Google Display's full list of 20 uploadable sizes, file limits and the five sizes to build first.
body_markdown:
## The short answer


- The standard banner ad sizes most advertisers build first are **300 x 250** (inline rectangle), **728 x 90** (leaderboard), **300 x 600** (half-page), **160 x 600** (wide skyscraper) and **320 x 50** (mobile banner).
- Google Ads lets you upload 20 display sizes, from 200 x 200 to 970 x 250 and 300 x 1050, as GIF, JPG or PNG up to 150 KB.
- Animated GIFs on Google must run 30 seconds or less and slower than 5 frames per second.
- If you do not want to build every size, a responsive display ad lets Google assemble your assets to fit almost any slot.


## Standard banner ad sizes


A banner ad is a display ad in a fixed rectangle on a web page or in an app. Its size is set in pixels, width first. The industry settled on a short list of sizes years ago because publishers build their page layouts around them, so a handful of sizes covers most of the inventory you can buy.


Start with five:


Size (px) Name Where it sits Why build it


300 x 250 Inline rectangle (medium rectangle) Inside articles and sidebars, desktop and mobile Fits the most slots


728 x 90 Leaderboard Top of desktop pages Standard header slot


300 x 600 Half-page ad Sidebar, desktop More room for a message and image


160 x 600 Wide skyscraper Narrow sidebar, desktop Common on older page layouts


320 x 50 Mobile banner Top or bottom of mobile pages and apps The standard mobile strip


The IAB publishes creative guidelines for display advertising, and Google lists the sizes it accepts on the Google Display Network. The full Google list is below. Names in the table follow the Google Ads Help page "Uploaded display ads specifications", checked on November 9, 2026. Which sizes get the most inventory depends on the network and the publishers, so check delivery by size in your reports before you commit to producing all of them.

## File rules for uploaded display ads


From the same Google Ads Help page:


Rule Limit


File types GIF, JPG, PNG


Maximum file size 150 KB


Animation length 30 seconds or shorter. Loops must stop after 30 seconds.


Animation speed Animated GIFs must be slower than 5 frames per second


AMPHTML and HTML5 bundles ZIP file; AMPHTML ads up to 600 KB compressed, with a single HTML document and up to 39 media assets


HTML5 access Account open more than 90 days, more than $9,000 USD lifetime spend, good policy history


The 150 KB cap is the one that bites. A 970 x 250 billboard with a photo needs aggressive compression. Export as JPG for photos, PNG for flat graphics with text, and check the weight before you upload. For animation ideas within these limits, see[animated ads](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/animated-ads) .


## Responsive display ads as a shortcut


Google says responsive display ads fit almost anywhere across the Display Network. You supply images, headlines, a logo and descriptions, and Google builds the ad to suit each slot. It also notes that even if you upload your own ads, you may still want responsive ads for spaces your custom sizes do not fit.


The trade-off is control. With uploaded sizes you decide exactly how each ad looks. With responsive you give up some of that for coverage. A practical split is to upload the five standard sizes for your best creative and let a responsive ad pick up the rest.


## Design rules that hold at every size


- **One message.** A 320 x 50 strip leaves room for about five words and a button. Cut the message to fit, do not shrink the type.
- **Logo and call to action visible in the first frame.** Do not wait for the animation to show them.
- **High-contrast text.** Banners sit on busy pages. Put text on a solid block, not on a photo.
- **Border on white backgrounds.** A thin border keeps a white banner from melting into a white page.
- **Design the biggest first.** Build 300 x 250 and 300 x 600, then adapt down to 320 x 50.
- **Keep type legible.** Check at the actual pixel size on a phone, not zoomed in.


## Banner sizes and social sizes are different


Do not reuse a display banner on social. Social placements use ratios such as 1:1, 4:5 and 9:16 and have their own safe zones. For Meta, see[Facebook ad sizes](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/facebook-ad-sizes) . Full-screen placements between content follow different rules again, covered in[interstitial ads](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/interstitial-ads) . And if your goal is reach rather than clicks, read[awareness campaign](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/awareness-campaign) before choosing the placements.

## Frequently asked questions


### What are the standard banner ad sizes?


The usual first builds are 300 x 250 (inline rectangle), 728 x 90 (leaderboard), 300 x 600 (half-page), 160 x 600 (wide skyscraper) and 320 x 50 (mobile banner). They match common publisher page layouts.


### What display ad sizes does Google Ads support?


For uploaded image ads Google lists 20 sizes, from 200 x 200 and 240 x 400 up to 970 x 250, 980 x 120 and 300 x 1050, plus mobile sizes 300 x 50, 320 x 50 and 320 x 100. The Google Ads Help page "Uploaded display ads specifications" has the full list.


### What is the maximum file size for a Google display ad?


150 KB for GIF, JPG and PNG image ads. Animated GIFs must be 30 seconds or shorter and slower than 5 frames per second.


### What is the best banner ad size?


There is no single best size. 300 x 250 fits the most placements and is the usual first build. Check delivery and conversions by size in your own reports, then put production time into the sizes that perform.


### What size is a mobile banner ad?


Google lists three mobile banner sizes: 300 x 50, 320 x 50 and 320 x 100 (large mobile banner). 320 x 50 is the common standard.


### Do I need to make every banner size?


No. You can build the five standard sizes yourself and let a responsive display ad cover the remaining slots. Google says responsive display ads fit almost anywhere on the Display Network.
